Building the 2027 roster

Toronto Tempo — where the team is short, and the player profiles worth discussing

Author

Hugo Leligny

Published

November 8, 2026

Part 2 of Availability wins. Independent analysis built on public data only (ESPN via SportsDataverse). Not affiliated with the Toronto Tempo or the WNBA. The staff knows things this analysis cannot see (medical information, internal load, game plans): read it as what the public data suggests, and as questions worth discussing, not as answers.

TipGlossary: the stats used in this report
  • FG% (field goal %): share of shots made. 4 made out of 10 = 40%.
  • eFG% (effective field goal %): like FG%, but a made 3-pointer counts as 1.5 made shots, because it is worth 3 points instead of 2. Formula: (made shots + 0.5 × made 3s) ÷ shots. Example: 10 shots, 4 made including 2 threes → FG% 40%, eFG% (4 + 1) ÷ 10 = 50%. It measures shooting quality in one number.
  • Points per shot (pps): average points scored per shot attempt (free throws excluded). 1.00 = 1 point per shot.
  • TOV% (turnover rate): turnovers per 100 possessions.
  • OREB% / DREB%: share of available offensive / defensive rebounds the team grabbed.
  • FT rate: free throws made per 100 shot attempts. It measures how often a team gets to the line.
  • SD (standard deviation): the usual spread between the 15 teams. A gap of −2 SD is very large, −1 SD is clear, −0.3 SD is small.
  • Per 36 minutes: a player’s totals scaled to 36 minutes, to compare players with different playing time.
  • Assisted / unassisted: a made shot is assisted when it follows a pass credited as an assist.

Summary

Part 1 showed that injuries, not travel, decided Toronto’s first season. This part looks at the roster itself: compared with the eight playoff teams, where is Toronto short, and what type of player could help close the gap?

  • Toronto is below playoff level at both ends, but furthest behind on defense. On offense, the gaps are moderate: shooting and turnovers are about one standard deviation below the playoff teams. On defense, they are twice as large: opponents shot 54.7% eFG against Toronto (worst in the league), and Toronto grabbed only 70.6% of defensive rebounds (14th of 15).
  • Opponents got to the rim: 34% of their shots against Toronto, compared with 26% against playoff teams.
  • Toronto’s offense relied on four creators, and three of them missed long stretches. Without them, the finishers had nobody to set them up.
  • Two profiles worth discussing, both durable (85%+ of games played): first, an interior defender who protects the rim and secures defensive rebounds; second, a backcourt creator who scores and passes, so the offense survives an injury.

1. Toronto’s biggest gaps are on defense

The four factors (shooting, turnovers, rebounding, free throws) explain most wins. Each one is measured twice: for Toronto’s offense, and for what Toronto allows on defense.

Factor Offense: what Toronto does Defense: what Toronto allows or wins
Shooting eFG%: shooting % with a 3 worth 1.5 made shots Opp. eFG%: the same, for opponents
Ball security Turnovers per 100 possessions (lower is better) Opp. turnovers per 100 possessions forced (higher is better)
Rebounding OREB%: share of Toronto’s missed shots that Toronto rebounds DREB%: share of opponents’ missed shots that Toronto rebounds
Free throws Free throws made per 100 shots: how often Toronto gets to the line and scores there Opp. free throws made per 100 shots: how often Toronto fouls (lower is better)

How to read the chart: the columns on the right give the raw value for Toronto, the average of the 8 playoff teams, and Toronto’s rank out of 15. The bar is the gap between Toronto and the playoff teams, always oriented so that left = worse. To compare gaps of different kinds (percentages, rates), I express each one in standard deviations (SD), the usual spread between the 15 teams: −1 SD is a clear gap, −2 SD a very large one.

  • Offense: moderate gaps. Shooting (eFG% 50.4% vs 52.8%) and turnovers (15.9% vs 14.6% of possessions) are about 1 SD below the playoff teams. Offensive rebounding and free throws are at playoff level.
  • Defense: the two biggest gaps. Opponents’ shooting against Toronto (54.7% eFG, worst in the league) is 2.2 SD behind the playoff teams. Defensive rebounding (70.6%, 14th) is 2.1 SD behind. Toronto also forced few turnovers (−1.1 SD).

So both ends need work, but a player who helps close the defensive gaps could move the team furthest.

2. Opponents got to the rim

How to read the chart: bordeaux = Toronto, blue = the 8 playoff teams. The left column is the shots Toronto took; the right column is the shots Toronto allowed (taken by opponents against Toronto, compared with opponents against the playoff teams). The top row shows where the shots were taken: the share of all attempts, made or missed, from each zone. The bottom row shows how often they went in (FG%). Zones are the same as in the individual shot charts below: rim within 4 feet of the basket, paint 4–14 feet, mid-range = longer 2-pointers, then corner and above-the-break 3s.

34% of opponents’ shots against Toronto came at the rim (within 4 feet of the basket), compared with 26% against playoff teams. Opponents took about 71 shots per game against Toronto, so that is roughly 5 to 6 more shots at the rim every game. These are the most efficient shots in basketball: opponents made 66% of them against Toronto (1.32 points per shot), vs about 40% in the paint or mid-range. With the playoff teams’ shot mix, Toronto would have conceded about 3 points fewer per game. Opponents also took more corner 3s (12% vs 10%) and scored more on them (1.15 points per shot). On offense, Toronto attacked the rim often (31% of its shots) but finished less well than playoff teams (61% vs 66%).

3. Player by player: where and how each one scores

Where each player scores efficiently

Each zone is coloured by the player’s points per shot compared with the league average in that zone. Blue = more efficient, grey = league level, bordeaux = less efficient. Each zone has two numbers: on top, the share of her shots taken there (where she shoots); below, her FG% there (how often she scores). For example, Mabrey takes 37% of her shots from above-the-break 3 and makes 38% of them. The colour uses points per shot rather than FG%, so that a 3-pointer counts for its real value.

  • Nyara Sabally is the most efficient scorer of the group (eFG 57%). Almost half of her shots come at the rim, where she converts 65%.
  • Kiki Rice is efficient in the mid-range (52%) and at league level at the rim, but struggles in the paint between the two (26%).
  • Laura Juskaite takes 41% of her shots at the rim, at league level, and is efficient from the corners (44%).
  • Kia Nurse takes 67% of her shots from three, at an average level. Her paint shots are rare and inefficient.

How each player creates her shots

The play-by-play also tells how each shot was created: a drive, a cut or putback, a shot off the dribble or from the post, or a spot-up jumper (mostly catch-and-shoot). It also tells whether a made shot was assisted.

  • Self-creators: Brittney Sykes and Kiki Rice. Only 37% and 43% of their made shots were assisted, and about two-thirds of their shots are drives or shots off the dribble. Losing Sykes in June removed the team’s main shot creator.
  • Finishers: Kia Nurse (88% assisted, 60% spot-up jumpers), Maria Conde (85%) and Isabelle Harrison (82%) depend on teammates to create for them.
  • Marina Mabrey is the most varied scorer: 44% of her shots off the dribble, 31% spot-up.

Who creates for the team

Finishers need someone to put them in position. To measure creation, I add up for each player the points of her own unassisted baskets (bordeaux) and the points of the baskets she assisted (blue), per 36 minutes. Next to each bar: the number of games she missed through injury or illness, out of 44. The right panel counts Toronto’s baskets scored without an assist per game, in four stretches of the season depending on whether Sykes and Rice were available. It shows how much the team could still create on its own.

  • Four players created Toronto’s offense: Sykes (19.7 points created per 36 min), Mabrey (19.0), Allemand (19.0, mostly by passing: 6.9 assists per 36) and Rice (18.3). Nobody else reaches 11.
  • Three of the four missed long stretches: Sykes 26 games, Rice 15, Mabrey 11.
  • Self-created baskets dropped as soon as one of them was missing: 11.6 unassisted baskets per game when Sykes and Rice both played, and about 9.5 after.

Toronto’s offense depended on a few creators with no cover behind them. When they were out, the finishers were still there, but nobody could put them in position.

4. Two profiles to consider, both durable

First profile: a durable interior defender

The two biggest gaps point to one player type: an interior defender (center or power forward) who protects the rim and secures defensive rebounds. Opponents got too many shots at the rim (section 2) and too many second chances (DREB%, 14th). A rim protector who also rebounds attacks both at once: she makes rim shots harder, and she ends the defensive possession with the rebound.

How to read the chart: each dot is a WNBA player with at least 400 minutes in 2026. Further right = more defensive rebounds per 36 minutes; higher = more blocks per 36 minutes, so the profile sits top right. The bigger the dot, the more games she played from 2024 to 2026. The blue players are the 12 best on a combined score (her league percentile in rebounds and in blocks, equal weight), among players available for at least 85% of their team’s games. Toronto’s players are mostly in the lower-left. Harrison and Key are the closest to the profile.

Given the rest of this report, I add one more criterion: availability. Each player’s share of her team’s games played from 2024 to 2026 (dot size). After a season decided by injuries, a player who is on the court 85–90% of the time is worth more than a slightly better player who misses a third of the season.

Some of the blue players are franchise players who will not move. The point is the profile and the method. With the club’s information (contracts, budget, medical records, scouting), the same table becomes a real shortlist.

From the chart, a few examples at different stages of a career. All of them combine strong defensive rebounding and rim protection with high availability over 2024–2026:

I have not checked contracts or free agency: these are examples of the profile, not a list of targets. The table also shows why availability belongs in the scoring. Brittney Griner, for example, still blocks 2.5 shots per 36 minutes but played 68% of her team’s games over the period.

Second profile: a durable backcourt creator

The creation analysis points to a second need: a guard who creates for herself and for others, so the offense does not depend on one or two players. The same method ranks the league on points created per 36 minutes, with few turnovers and high availability:

Player 2026 team Points created / 36 min Assists / 36 min Turnovers / 36 min Availability 2024–26
Veronica Burton Golden State (champion) 23.1 7.2 1.8 93%
Natisha Hiedeman Seattle 21.7 6.0 2.7 97%
Erica Wheeler Los Angeles 20.8 7.0 2.5 98%
Natasha Cloud Chicago 19.8 6.2 2.7 93%
For reference: Brittney Sykes Toronto 19.7 4.1 2.6 played 17 of 44 games in 2026

Same caution as above: contracts not checked, examples of the profile only. The priority order matters: the defensive gap is the largest, so the interior defender comes first. The creator is the insurance that keeps the offense alive when injuries hit, as they did in 2026.

Next step: the draft and international players

An expansion team builds through the draft and international recruitment as much as through free agency. The same method applies there:

  • NCAA: the same public source (SportsDataverse) publishes women’s college basketball box scores and play-by-play. The pipeline can ingest them with the same scripts, rank prospects on the same defensive profile, and add availability over their college career.
  • International leagues (EuroLeague Women, national leagues, FIBA competitions): data is less standardised. Building one clean table from several sources is exactly the reconciliation work a data engineer does.
  • Canada: as the league’s first Canadian team, Toronto has a natural interest in Canadian prospects. The same profile can be screened among U SPORTS, NCAA and national-team players.

Method and limits

  • Four factors computed from team box scores; shot zones from ESPN shot coordinates (rim within 4 ft, paint 4–14 ft).
  • Candidate scores combine defensive rebounds and blocks per 36 minutes (league percentiles); availability = share of her team’s regular-season games played, 2024–2026.
  • Box-score stats measure what a defender finishes (a rebound, a block), not everything she prevents. With tracking data I would add rim deterrence (opponent shots near her), switching and matchup data.
  • Contracts, salary cap and medical files are not public: the shortlist step belongs to the club.
